vignette:
She is a 38-year-old woman who works as a stock broker in a high-rise office in the financial district. Her desk faces a window that overlooks a busy intersection, and she keeps the blinds open because she needs to feel the rhythm of the city below—the movement of people, the flow of traffic, the constant noise. She tells herself it helps her think. But the truth is, she needs to see who is coming.

It started two years ago. A former client from her early days in brokerage, a man in his mid-fifties who had invested modestly and then blamed her when the market dipped. He began sending emails—first just angry, then strangely detailed. He described her outfits from the day before, the color of her scarf, the route she took to the elevator. She reported it to building security, changed her commute, ignored the messages. That made it worse. He started showing up. Outside her gym, at the grocery store she used on weekends, once in the lobby of her apartment building pretending to buzz a friend. He never threatened her directly, never touched her, but his presence was constant, an unblinking eye in the corner of her life.

She changed her phone number, moved to a new apartment, switched firms. The stalking stopped after about six months—he lost interest, or found another target, she doesn’t know. But the feeling never stopped.

Now, when she walks into the office each morning at 6:30 AM, she scans the faces of the early-shift security guards, the janitors, the few colleagues already at their desks. She checks the stairwell doors are locked. She sits with her back to the wall in the break room. At her desk, she has arranged her monitors so she can see the hallway mirror and the entrance to the trading floor. It is not paranoia, she insists—it’s being prepared. It’s what keeps her ahead of the market, too: always scanning, always anticipating the next unexpected move. She used to be known for her cool head and rapid decisions. Now she freezes when an unfamiliar number flashes on her phone. She double-checks her lock screen three times before leaving the office. She has stopped taking the subway. She spends an extra forty minutes each way in ride-shares, paying more attention to the driver’s face in the rearview mirror than to the market reports on her tablet.

Her partner, a graphic designer, tries to help. He has installed extra locks on the doors, a video doorbell, motion-sensor lights. He tells her she’s safe now. She nods and smiles, but at night she lies awake listening for the scrape of a shoe on the pavement outside, the click of a lock being tampered with. She has not slept through the night in eighteen months. Her body is wired, always tight: her shoulders hunched, her jaw clenched, her hands cold even when the heating is on. She drinks too much coffee, smokes occasionally when she is alone on the fire escape, and has lost eight pounds she did not have to lose.

Last week, during a routine video call with a client, the lighting in his background reflected off a window and briefly cast a shadow that looked like a figure standing behind him. She went silent for ten seconds, then excused herself and ended the call. She sat in the bathroom stall for fifteen minutes, sweating, heart pounding, telling herself to breathe. She thought she had pushed him away, but now she wonders if he is still there, waiting for her to let her guard down.

She still performs at work—just well enough to keep her job. But she no longer trusts her own instincts. She second-guesses trades she would have made without thinking. She spends more time on her phone checking the street cameras outside her building than on the Bloomberg Terminal. She knows this is not sustainable. She knows something is wrong. But when she tries to explain it to herself, all she can say is that she is still being watched, even when no one is there.
